answer.rationale: Binding constraint is continuity: the contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew, the line is at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer, and I get one decision. A primary-vendor switch (memory_c2) or a new second-source qualification (memory_c3) cannot be stood up inside 14 days without raising delivery risk, which the objective forbids; defer_decision leaves the line without a contracted supply after day 85; straight negotiate_terms is already foreclosed because the incumbent refused to reopen price this cycle. That leaves renewal, and memory_c6 is the only inherited path to cost reduction that does not require the incumbent to reopen price this cycle: term length, not unit price, is the lever. So memory_c6 is the load-bearing memory and the one I spend the single verification on. What I need from the source record: whether the volume pricing was actually attributable to term length rather than a one-off volume spike or a category where we held leverage we no longer have, and what the realized discount was against an 18% mandate. Standing uncertainty I am not resolving: memory_c2's cost win may well be real and larger than any term discount, but it is unverified in this context (unknown category, unknown criticality, unknown ramp time) and I am declining it on timing, not on merit; memory_c1's stability claim and memory_c4's benchmarking win are both plausible but stale and unverified here. Downstream value risk, flagged explicitly: a multi-year commitment buys this cycle's cost relief by spending future optionality. It directly forecloses the memory_c2 switch and constrains the memory_c3 dual-source move that a 94%-utilization single-source line clearly needs, and it hands the next agent a locked position they cannot revisit. If memory_c6's record does not substantiate a term-driven discount near the mandate, I will not lengthen the term to chase it. Scale is therefore a bounded renewal, not a broad rollout: shortest term that still triggers the volume tier, an explicit carve-out permitting a qualified second source, and a benchmark/reopener clause so the next review inherits room to move. I expect this to close part, not all, of the 18% gap, and I would rather report a partial cost result honestly than protect a line running with no buffer.
